title: How to Preach With Skeptics in the Room
subtitle: A guide to apologetic preaching with skeptics and seekers in the room, anticipating objections, honoring doubt, and commending the faith without dumbing down the gospel.

sections.title: Assume the Doubter Is Listening
sections.body:
Someone in your room does not believe a word of it. Preach as though you know that, because you should.

The dragged-along spouse. The college student home for the weekend who lost his faith in the fall. The grieving father who came because his wife asked and is sitting there furious at a God he is not sure exists. The lifelong member who has never told a soul that the whole thing went hollow years ago. They are all in the room, and most preaching acts as if they are not, as if everyone present already shares the assumptions, already grants the premises, already says amen on cue. That preaching is a conversation among insiders, overheard by outsiders who conclude, correctly, that it was not meant for them.

I came to faith out of atheism. I remember exactly what it was to sit in a church and feel like a tourist in someone else's certainty. The preacher who forgets that listener is preaching to the converted and wondering why the lost never stay.

sections.title: Take the Objection Seriously
sections.body:
Nothing closes a skeptic faster than a preacher who knocks down an objection no thinking person actually holds.

We build a straw atheist, a cartoon of unbelief, and we demolish him to the satisfaction of the people who already agree. The real skeptic in the fourth row watches this and concludes you have never met anyone like him and never read anyone who thinks. You have confirmed his suspicion that faith only survives where it does not have to face the strongest form of the question. Do the opposite. State the objection better than the doubter could state it himself. Name the problem of suffering without flinching. Admit the church's record where it is damning. Grant the hard thing before you answer it.

This is not weakness. It is the only thing that earns a hearing. When a skeptic hears you describe his own doubt more honestly than he has heard it described in church before, something shifts. He stops defending and starts listening, because for the first time he believes you are not afraid of the truth.

sections.title: Skeptics Are Not Looking for Easy
sections.body:
The instinct is to soften the message for the doubter, to trim the hard edges, to make the gospel small enough to swallow. This is exactly backward.

The skeptic did not leave the faith because it asked too much. He left because it seemed too small, a tame thing for nice people, a set of life tips with a steeple on top. Give him that watered-down version and you have only confirmed why he walked. What stops a serious unbeliever is a serious gospel, the strange and difficult and enormous claim that the God who made the universe entered it and was killed by it and rose. That is not embarrassing to a skeptic. It is interesting. The crucified God is a stumbling block, but it is a stumbling block worth tripping over, and the watered-down version is not worth crossing the street for.

Do not protect the doubter from the depth. The depth is the draw. Preach the whole strange truth, and trust that the thing that has held thinking minds for two thousand years can hold the one in your room.

sections.title: Argue Without Sounding Like a Lawyer
sections.body:
The skeptic does not need a debate handout dropped into the middle of your sermon. He needs the case woven into the preaching of the text.

The clumsy way is to stop the sermon, announce a section on the evidence, recite four arguments for the resurrection, and resume. It feels bolted on because it is. The better way is to anticipate the objection at the moment the text raises it and to answer it as you go, briefly, fairly, and then keep moving. When the passage speaks of the resurrection, you take ten seconds to acknowledge that this is the claim everything stands or falls on, and that the men who first told it died refusing to take it back. You are not pausing to argue. You are preaching with the doubter's question always in your peripheral vision.

Keller called this disarming the skeptic by addressing the question he was already asking. Speak to the objection before the doubter can raise it, and you have shown him you are not hiding from it. That is worth more than any single proof.

sections.title: You Are Not Closing a Sale
sections.body:
The aim is not to win the argument on Sunday. It is to make the faith credible enough that the skeptic comes back.

No one is reasoned into the kingdom in a single sermon, and the preacher who treats the doubter as a deal to close will only push him away. Your job is smaller and more patient than conversion. Your job is to remove the false reasons for unbelief, to show the skeptic that the faith is not what he thought, that it can face his hardest question without panic, that the people who hold it are not fools. You are clearing the ground so that the real question, the question of the heart and not just the head, can finally be asked. The Spirit converts. You commend.

So preach the skeptic a faith big enough to doubt and strong enough to hold. Send him home unable to dismiss it as easily as he came. That is not failure. That is the long, slow work of opening a closed door. Leave it open.
